oneSentence: A set of step-by-step instructions for turning inputs into an output or action.
plainExplanation:
An algorithm tells a computer or a person what to do, in what order, to reach a result. The input is the information it starts with. The output is the answer, label, ranking or action it produces.

Some algorithms are simple and fixed. For example, they may sort names from A to Z or check whether a number is larger than 100. Others are more complex and use many steps, conditions and calculations.

An algorithm is not the same as artificial intelligence. Many algorithms have nothing to do with AI. A calculator, a spam filter based on fixed rules, and a route planner all use algorithms, but they work in different ways.

A model is also different from an algorithm. A model is a mathematical pattern learned from data. An algorithm may be used to train a model, and another algorithm may use that model later to produce an output.

everydayAnalogy.title: Sorting paper forms at a service desk
everydayAnalogy.story: At a service desk, staff receive printed forms from many organisations. One clerk first checks the logo at the top, then looks for the page layout, then compares the photo of the form with a folder of standard templates. If the logo and layout match Template B, the clerk places the form in the blue tray; if not, the clerk sends it for manual review. Everyone follows the same checklist in the same order.

mapping.aiElement: the ordered steps of an algorithm
reference patterns or rules used during processing

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A human clerk can use broad judgement and may notice unusual context that was never written down. Many algorithms cannot do that unless such rules or learned patterns were built into the system, and some algorithms work through numerical calculations rather than explicit checklist steps.

visual.title: How an algorithm turns input into an output
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to say that an algorithm takes input, applies ordered steps or rules, and produces an output.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four boxes connected by arrows. Box 1 shows a document icon labelled 'Input'. Box 2 shows a magnifying glass and checklist labelled 'Read features'. Box 3 shows a decision diamond and ruler labelled 'Apply rules or calculations'. Box 4 shows two stacked trays labelled 'Output: template match or review'. Small text under the arrows says 'same steps each time, unless the algorithm includes branching conditions'.

steps.label: Input arrives
steps.explanation: The process starts with information such as text, numbers, an image or a click.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box on the left with icons for text, numbers and an image. Add the label 'Input'.

steps.label: Relevant parts are identified
steps.explanation: The algorithm uses the parts it needs, such as keywords, sizes, dates or layout features.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a second box with a document and highlighted sections. Label it 'Read features'.

steps.label: Rules or calculations are applied
steps.explanation: The algorithm follows ordered instructions. Some steps are fixed rules; some involve mathematical calculations.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a third box with a checklist and a simple decision diamond. Label it 'Apply steps'.

steps.label: Result is produced
steps.explanation: The output may be a label, score, ranking, prediction or action.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a final box with two output trays labelled 'Template B' and 'Manual review'. Label the box 'Output'.

visual.interaction: On hover or tap, each box reveals one example input and output: a photographed form goes in; the result is either 'matches template B' or 'send for review'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains an algorithm as a four-stage flow. First, input arrives, such as text, numbers or an image. Second, the system identifies the relevant parts, such as keywords, dates or layout features. Third, it applies ordered rules or calculations, sometimes with branches such as yes or no checks. Fourth, it produces an output, such as a label, score, ranking or next action. The main point is that an algorithm is a process for transforming input into output through defined steps.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-box flowchart shows Input, Read features, Apply steps, and Output, with arrows between them and brief example labels under each box.

workedExample.scenario: Matching a photographed paper form to the right template
workedExample.input: Photo of a form with the logo 'Health Office', two boxes at the top, and a barcode in the bottom-right corner.
process: The system receives the photo and measures visible features such as logo position, page layout and barcode location.
It compares those features with three stored templates: A, B and C.
Template B matches the logo position, the two top boxes and the barcode location more closely than the others.
Because the match score for Template B is above the review threshold, the system assigns the label 'Template B'.
workedExample.result: The form is routed to the Template B processing queue instead of being sent for manual sorting.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A country office uses an approved internal tool to triage a shared inbox by sorting messages into categories such as procurement, travel, IT support and general enquiries.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: This helps staff see that the tool is using an algorithm: it takes email subject lines and approved metadata as input, applies rules or learned patterns, and sends each message to the most suitable queue.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not send confidential, personal, protection-sensitive or security-sensitive email content to an unapproved public AI service for triage; use approved systems and keep human oversight for unclear or high-risk cases.

whyItMatters: If you hear that a system uses an algorithm, you can ask useful questions: what inputs it uses, what steps it follows, what output it produces, and where errors or unfair effects might appear.

commonMisconceptions.correction: AI systems use algorithms, but many ordinary software tools use algorithms too. The word is broader than AI.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: An algorithm is always objective and neutral.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The steps may be precise, but the choice of inputs, rules, thresholds and training data can still reflect human assumptions and create biased results.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: An algorithm is the same thing as a model.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A model is usually a learned mathematical structure. An algorithm is the procedure that may train a model, run a model or do something without any model at all.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: An algorithm is a clear method for taking some information in and producing an answer or action out.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: An algorithm is a finite, ordered procedure that maps input to output through defined operations such as comparisons, branching, iteration and numerical computation.

keyTakeaway: An algorithm is the method; it is not automatically AI, and it is not the same as a model.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes an algorithm?
options: A machine that stores all the data in an AI system
A step-by-step procedure that transforms input into an output
A guarantee that a computer system will be fair and accurate
A name used only for advanced AI systems
quickCheck.explanation: An algorithm is a procedure or set of instructions. It can be simple or complex, and it exists in many kinds of software, not only AI. Being algorithmic does not guarantee fairness or accuracy.
